cards.title: Recession-Proof Product Selection for Amazon
cards.summary: Pick Amazon product categories whose demand holds up in downturns instead of freezing on recession fear.
cards.use_when: Deciding which product categories to source or launch when you're worried about a recession or soft consumer spending.
steps: Accept the source's view that a recession is a 5-out-of-10 concern: some categories drop in sales, but others stay resilient.
Weight categories the source names as recession-resistant: groceries, baby items, pet products and small-pleasure items like candy.
Treat this as directional, not a rule: verify current demand with keyword/search-volume tools before committing capital.
Do not let uncertainty become analysis paralysis — the source says every year people predict collapse and most never start.
Size your first order so a soft launch doesn't sink you rather than betting the farm on a macro call.
caveats: The presenter rates recession risk 5/10 and admits nobody actually knows; category lists are his opinion, not researched benchmarks.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Financing an Amazon Launch With Pre-Sales
cards.summary: Raise production funds from pre-sales instead of paying startup costs out of pocket.
cards.use_when: You want to start an Amazon FBA business but don't have capital for inventory.
steps: Validate interest in your product before producing anything, e.g. by collecting demand signals on social media or via a crowdfunding page.
Collect payment or committed orders up front and use that cash to fund the first production run — the source says AJ started with zero dollars this way.
Treat startup capital as variable, not fixed: audience-reported bands range from under $500 (11% of sellers) to over $10,000 (22%), so pick a scale you can fund.
Use campaign supporters as your first buyers and reviewers at launch, which also helps early sales velocity.
caveats: Pre-sale cash flow only works if you can actually deliver; delays (see the source's 4→8-week manufacturer slips) can turn pre-sales into refunds or angry backers.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Modeling Amazon Fees and FBA Fulfillment
cards.summary: Understand the 15% referral fee, monthly plan choice and per-unit FBA cost before pricing your product.
cards.use_when: Building unit economics or deciding between FBA and self-fulfillment for a new Amazon product.
steps: Account for the 15% Amazon referral fee on every sale; the source frames it as marketing cost versus the billions Amazon spends acquiring customers.
Choose plan: individual seller is free but adds $0.99 per item, so professional at $39.99/month makes sense above roughly 40 units/month.
Use FBA so your items are Prime-eligible — the source claims Prime products sell about 5x more than non-Prime (his own FBM→FBA switch).
Budget FBA pick-and-pack per unit by size: ~$4/unit for the source's electrolyte product; heavier items cost more.
Compare FBA fee to your own shipping + labor instead of treating it as pure loss; the source says it was equivalent to his own shipping cost without the work.
caveats: Fee percentages and FBA rates change — verify current Amazon fee schedules in Seller Central. The 5x sales lift is one seller's anecdote, not a benchmark.
Brand referral program was cited as reducing the fee from 15% to 5%; confirm current eligibility before relying on it.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Estimate Monthly Product Revenue From BSR
cards.summary: Convert a competitor's Amazon best-seller rank into estimated monthly units and revenue before entering a niche.
cards.use_when: Sizing demand and revenue potential for a product idea or category before sourcing.
steps: Open Amazon Best Sellers in your target category to find top-ranked products.
Record the product's Best Sellers Rank (BSR) number and its price.
Enter marketplace, category and BSR into a free sales estimator (the source uses Jungle Scout's) to get estimated monthly units.
Multiply estimated units by price to approximate monthly revenue — the source's examples: pimple patch ~170k units ≈ $1.9M/month; sports-nutrition #1 ~145k units ≈ $3M/month.
Cross-check at the category level: the source notes 4 of the top 8 bestselling supplements were electrolyte powders, several doing $1–3M/month.
caveats: BSR-to-sales estimates are third-party approximations and drift by category and season; treat as a screening range, not a forecast.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Keyword Mining for Product Gaps With Helium 10 Magnet
cards.summary: Find underserved search terms with real volume and no exact-match product, then build your product around them.
cards.use_when: Choosing a specific product to launch, or validating that a niche has a keyword gap you can own.
steps: Enter an interest or niche (e.g. 'carnivore diet', 'caffeinated gum') into Helium 10's Magnet tool and pull keyword data.
Sort by the Magnet IQ/opportunity score and scan the list; the source spent ~30 minutes reviewing candidates.
For each promising keyword, search it on Amazon and check whether any product exactly matches the search.

Target keywords with meaningful monthly search volume but no perfect-match listing (source example: 'carnivore electrolytes' ~2,000 searches/month with only sugar-laden or flavored electrolytes ranking).
Also look for smaller long-tail terms with lower competition (e.g. 'gym gum', 'workout gum') to center your title and listing around.
caveats: Search volumes are tool estimates and shift over time (the source saw 'caffeinated gum' spike from ~2,000 to ~15,000/month later). Verify current demand in Seller Central/tools before ordering inventory.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Search-First Product Framing: Amazon Is a Search Engine
cards.summary: Design your product and title around an exact search phrase buyers already type, not around what you want to make.
cards.use_when: Naming a product, writing a listing title, or deciding whether a product idea can win on Amazon.
steps: Treat Amazon as a search engine: buyers type a query and see image results, so your job is to match an existing query with a distinct product.
Name your product the exact search phrase when it's descriptive (the source named his product 'Carnivore Electrolytes' so searchers immediately recognize fit).
Build the title around your validated core keyword(s) so Amazon associates your listing with that query.
Confirm the query has unsatisfied demand — the source's test was 'is anyone selling a product that perfectly matches this search?' If not, that's your opening.
caveats: Exact-match naming may hurt trademark distinctiveness; the source later emphasizes trademark/brand registry needs, so balance SEO naming against brandability.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Packaging Design for Category Contrast
cards.summary: Choose packaging colors that visually contrast the dominant colors on the search results page so your thumbnail gets clicked.
cards.use_when: Designing your product's packaging or main image to stand out against named competitors in Amazon search results.
steps: Search your target keyword on Amazon and screenshot the results grid to see the dominant colors.
Identify the emotional signal of those colors — the source says blues/whites/greens read as calming (insurance-like), red reads as high-energy (car/fast-food-like).
Deliberately invert: the source chose black packaging with red lettering for a supplement in a sea of blue, white and green competitors.
Apply contrast at thumbnail size — the decision happens in a grid of images, not on the product page.
Extend the palette consistently to logo, packaging and listing images so the click-through is reinforced at the PDP.
caveats: Color psychology is the source's heuristic, not a tested result; validate with your own search-results screenshot and category norms.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Sourcing Design Help at Four Price Tiers
cards.summary: Pick the right design vendor tier for logo and packaging based on budget and risk tolerance.
cards.use_when: Commissioning a logo, brand identity or Amazon packaging design for a new product.
steps: DIY free: Canva if you have design skill and no budget.
Cheapest: Fiverr, from ~$5, but 'you get what you pay for' — the source shows a $5 logo example.
Mid-tier: Upwork freelancers, ~$50 for a logo in the source's experience.
Crowdsourced: 99designs, ~$300, gets hundreds of submissions and lets you poll friends/family/pre-launch supporters before choosing.
Amazon-specific: the source recommends FBA Creatives (logos, brand, packaging built for Amazon) and used it for all his products.
caveats: A 99designs winner was flagged for brand infringement in the source's own story and 99designs offered no help — always run a basic trademark check on any chosen logo.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Opening an Amazon Seller Account
cards.summary: Set up the correct seller plan and gather the documents Amazon requires before you start the signup flow.
cards.use_when: Registering a new Amazon selling account and choosing between individual and professional plans.
steps: Go to sell.amazon.com and find the individual-seller signup option (the source notes it's hidden at the bottom of the page).
Choose individual (free) if you'll sell fewer than ~40 units/month; it adds $0.99 per item.
Choose professional ($39.99/month) if you expect more than 40 units/month — the source's own plan.
Have ready before starting: valid ID or passport, recent bank/credit-card statement, a credit card for the monthly fee, and a mobile phone number.
Provide business details and the bank account where Amazon will deposit your payouts.
caveats: Amazon's signup flow and UI change frequently — verify current steps and fees in Seller Central; $39.99/month is the source's figure at recording time.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Finding a Manufacturer for an Amazon Product
cards.summary: Choose among four sourcing channels based on whether your product is consumable and how fast you need a partner.
cards.use_when: Sourcing a manufacturer or private-label supplier for a new Amazon product.
steps: Alibaba.com — largest directory of overseas manufacturers (Asia/Europe/India).
ThomasNet.com — US-based manufacturers, useful when you want domestic production.
Google search 'your product + manufacturer' or '+ private labeler' — the source found his own manufacturer this way and notes many US manufacturers require large quantities.
Ask another seller who already makes a similar product who their manufacturer is — fastest route, and the route used in the 7-day challenge.
Match channel to product: for a consumable/ingestible, the source avoided China and used Google/ThomasNet and referrals for domestic production.
caveats: Referral-only sourcing depends on access to a seller network; without one, expect longer lead times. Verify certification/ingredient claims before ordering.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: First Production Run Sizing and Lead-Time Reality
cards.summary: Order a test-sized run against expected daily sales, and plan around multi-week manufacturing plus inbound lead times.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many units to order on your first production run and when to place reorders.
steps: Get tiered quotes: the source's manufacturer quoted $8/unit at 500 units and $7/unit at 2,000 — cheaper per unit at higher volume.
Estimate realistic daily sales, then size the order as roughly 3 months of that rate (the source guessed 3–4 units/day and ordered 500).
Ask for the production lead time up front and pad it: in the source's case it slipped from 4–6 weeks to 6–8 weeks, plus a couple more weeks for Amazon to receive and check in.
Time the launch to your category's peak season (the source targeted January for supplements because of New Year's resolutions).
Place reorders based on observed sell-through, not your original pessimism — repeated stockouts in the source's case came from underestimating demand.
caveats: Lead times vary widely by product and factory; the source's specific weeks are an example, and his own plans slipped repeatedly.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Building a Pre-Launch Audience and Launch-Day Velocity
cards.summary: Grow a small brand following before launch, then convert it into concentrated day-one sales and early reviews.
cards.use_when: Preparing to launch a new Amazon listing and needing early sales velocity to rank in search.
steps: Before launch, create Instagram and TikTok accounts for the brand and post content to accumulate followers.
For speed, the source spliced his product into existing viral niche videos (e.g. a 'what I eat on the carnivore diet' clip) rather than filming original content.
Collect emails from interested followers and email them leading up to and on launch day.
Offer a launch-week discount to convert that audience immediately: the source dropped his planned $24.99 price to $16.99 for week one.
Ask buyers for reviews (Amazon prohibits asking specifically for 5-star reviews) to build early social proof, which supports ranking.
caveats: Amazon prohibits incentivized or 5-star-solicited reviews; only ask neutrally. The presenter's own network promoting his product is not replicable for most sellers.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Creating and Publishing an Amazon Listing
cards.summary: Publish a listing with imagery, title, bullets and description before inventory arrives so the launch isn't delayed.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new product detail page in Seller Central, or preparing listing content in advance of inventory.
steps: In Seller Central, use the menu → 'Add a Product' → 'I'm adding a product not sold on Amazon' and pick your category.
Fill in title (with your validated core keyword), brand name, bullets and description.
Upload your prepared images and set price and other required attributes.
Do this while manufacturing finishes — the source completed his listing weeks before the product was ready, so launch only needed inventory.
Check Amazon's category-gating rules early: the source's 'carnivore diet'-related product was flagged and required a Certificate of Analysis (COA) from the manufacturer before approval.
caveats: Amazon UI labels and gating/COA requirements vary by category and change — verify current requirements in Seller Central before listing.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Inbound Shipping and Amazon Check-In Workflow
cards.summary: Send inventory to an Amazon fulfillment center in a way that gets checked in before you run out of stock.
cards.use_when: Shipping a production run to Amazon's warehouse and timing the handoff to your live listing.
steps: In Seller Central, open the product and choose Send/Replenish Inventory.
Enter box dimensions and the total number of units per box.
Print box labels, attach them to each carton, and drop the shipment with a carrier (the source used UPS).
Allow a couple of weeks for Amazon to receive and process the shipment before it's sellable.
Coordinate the check-in with your current stock run-out date — the source twice had inventory check in the day before running out.
caveats: Amazon's inbound workflow and label requirements change; verify current shipping requirements. Amazon may split or reject shipments, so build buffer time.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Launch-Week Discounting to Drive Rank
cards.summary: Discount aggressively in the first week to concentrate sales, then raise price once rank and reviews are established.
cards.use_when: Pricing a new Amazon product during its launch window.
steps: Set a launch-week discount below your intended long-term price (source: $16.99 launch vs. planned $24.99).
Tell your pre-launch audience the discount is time-limited to convert them early.
Expect thin margins during launch — the source made $75 profit on $500 of day-one revenue at the discounted price.
After the first week, raise to your target price; the source found sales held even as he moved $24.99 → $29.99 → $34.99.
Use the resulting reviews and rank as support for the higher price.
caveats: Discount depth and its ranking effect are source-specific; Amazon's ranking algorithm changes. Don't assume a discount guarantees rank.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Using Amazon PPC Without Eroding Profit
cards.summary: Advertise on Amazon to hold search position, but measure profit impact and be ready to turn spend down.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run or scale Amazon Sponsored Products, or when profit margins are being eaten by ad spend.
steps: Treat PPC as pay-per-click: you pay on clicks, not sales, so choose the search terms you bid on carefully — a bad target match spends money without converting.
Start PPC after you have some reviews (the source began after week one on his launch), so clicks convert better.
Track profit, not just revenue: the source's month-six test of turning PPC off kept sales roughly flat while raising profit.
Watch for the trap the source warns about — Amazon advertising can actually lower total profit if not carefully managed.
Reconcile PPC spend against organic rank gains and margin per unit before increasing bids.
caveats: Source data is a single product over six months; PPC results vary by category, price and competition. Not a universal rule to turn PPC off.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Avoid the Three Big Amazon Launch Mistakes
cards.summary: Price closer to category norms, order enough inventory, and launch sooner to avoid the source's biggest self-identified errors.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a go-to-market plan for a new Amazon product before committing spend.
steps: Price against category norms, not just your cost: the source priced at $24.99 from cost while competitors sold at $34.99, then found raising price didn't reduce sales.
Notice that a few dollars of price increase can multiply profit significantly — the source's monthly profit rose as price increased.
Order inventory sized to likely success, not your own doubt: repeated near-stockouts came from believing the product wouldn't sell well.
Run the replenishment math against the manufacturer's real lead time to avoid gaps (see stockout planning card).
Accept that waiting is the biggest cost: the source delayed his first product a year and estimates that cost him ~$100k in missed profit; every year he waited on new launches added to that.
caveats: 'Raise price, sales stay the same' is one seller's experience on one product; test price changes in your own niche.
The ~$100k cost-of-delay figure is an estimate, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Stockout Prevention and Inventory Buffer Planning
cards.summary: Match replenishment orders to observed sell-through and product seasonality so a growing listing never goes out of stock.
cards.use_when: Planning reorders for a product whose sales are accelerating, especially around peak season.
steps: Track units sold per month against stock on hand early (the source sold 288 of 500 units in month one and nearly stocked out).
Trigger a reorder the moment sell-through outpaces your original daily-rate assumption, not at a fixed calendar point.
Add together manufacturer lead time (source: 4–8 weeks), inbound shipping and Amazon check-in (weeks) when setting the reorder point.
Consider slowing demand with price increases as a short-term buffer — the source raised price from $24.99 to $34.99 across months two and three and sales held, which also reduced stockout risk.
Keep a review of actual outs versus your projections each month and adjust order size upward.
caveats: Price increases to slow demand are a stopgap; the source ultimately calls under-ordering a mistake, not a strategy.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Choosing a Product You're Passionate About
cards.summary: Anchor product selection in a niche you know and care about so you can spot a real gap competitors miss.
cards.use_when: Selecting which Amazon product category or product to develop from among many options.
steps: Pick a category you personally care about (the source chose health/supplements after trying the carnivore diet).
Study competitors in that niche to find a specific customer need none of them serves — for the source, that was electrolytes with no sugar or artificial flavors for carnivore dieters.
Use keyword data to confirm the niche has search demand before committing (see the Magnet/BSR cards).
Prefer a niche where you can explain why your product is the perfect fit for a defined searcher (e.g., 'carnivore electrolytes' buyers who are being served flavored, sugared products today).
Validate that the gap is real by ordering and testing competitor products before designing yours.
caveats: Passion alone isn't enough — the source pairs it with keyword validation and demand estimates; without demand, passion products don't sell.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Validating a Product Gap by Buying Competitors
cards.summary: Buy and test competing products to define a concrete improvement before formulation.
cards.use_when: Designing a differentiated product in a category you can physically test.
steps: Order a sample of competitors' products to evaluate them hands-on (the source spent ~$200 on competitor caffeine gum).
Identify a recurring weakness across all competitors — in the source's case, every caffeinated gum on the market tasted bad.
Make fixing that weakness the core design goal of your product (better taste for the source's gum; clean ingredients/flavor for the electrolytes).
Send samples to pre-launch supporters for feedback (the source sent ~100 units) on flavor, sweetness and strength before the full run.
Use the collected feedback to finalize the formulation, then scale to production.
caveats: Formulation for novel products can be expensive — the source paid $5,000 for custom gum formulation — and costs vary widely by category.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Trademark and Brand Registry Paths
cards.summary: File a trademark yourself first and only escalate to a lawyer on rejection to keep startup costs low.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to obtain trademark protection and Amazon Brand Registry eligibility for a new brand.
steps: Understand that a pending trademark is enough to apply for Amazon Brand Registry (per the source), so you don't need an approved mark first.
File the trademark yourself for the lower filing fee (the source paid ~$250) rather than paying a lawyer up front.
If the application is rejected, hire a lawyer at that point to respond — the source argues there's no reason to pay lawyer fees upfront.
Also consider an LLC for liability separation (the source paid ~$150) before you start selling publicly.
Check that the logo/name doesn't infringe an existing brand before filing (see the 99designs infringement story).
caveats: Trademark law, fees and Brand Registry rules vary by country and change; the source's figures are US examples — verify current USPTO/Amazon requirements before filing.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Realistic Amazon Business Cost Stack
cards.summary: Budget for the full set of costs — research tools, samples, design, legal, formulation, manufacturing and inbound — not just inventory.
cards.use_when: Building a startup budget for a new Amazon FBA product before committing capital.
steps: List likely cost lines before you start: research tool subscription, competitor samples, logo/packaging design, LLC, trademark, UPC barcodes with GS1, seller plan, formulation and first production run plus inbound shipping.

Use the source's example stack as a rough shape, not a target: ~$150 Helium 10, ~$200 competitor samples, ~$499 design, ~$150 LLC, ~$250 trademark, ~$20 UPCs, ~$49 seller account, ~$5,000 formulation, ~$16,000 production, ~$150 inbound.
Reduce cost where possible: raise pre-sale/crowdfunding funds (the source raised ~$2,000 on Kickstarter) and use referrals for sourcing.
Recognize that custom formulations and novel products cost far more than generic private-label products.
Keep a buffer for delays — longer lead times mean you may pay for a second run before the first one has sold through.
caveats: These are one seller's figures for a specific product in a specific year; your costs will differ by category, volume and supplier.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Reading Amazon Advertising and Fee Costs as Marketing
cards.summary: Frame Amazon's 15% referral fee and ad spend as the cost of access to Amazon's buyer base rather than pure loss.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether Amazon's fees make a product viable, or comparing Amazon to your own DTC channel.
steps: Note the source's framing: Amazon spent over $40 billion acquiring customers, and the 15% fee buys access to that demand.
Compare against alternatives — third-party marketing costs and the labor/shipping cost of self-fulfillment — before deciding the fee is too high.
Treat the fee as a percentage that scales with revenue rather than a fixed cost, so higher volume doesn't increase the rate.
Factor FBA fees and PPC into per-unit margin from the start so the 'Amazon takes so much' objection becomes a modeled number.
Track whether your total Amazon cost (referral + FBA + PPC) still leaves a workable margin at your price.
caveats: The $40B figure and 'cheaper than most marketing' claim are the source's; your margin math depends on your own pricing and category competition.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: One-Time Effort, Ongoing Passive Operations
cards.summary: Structure an FBA business so routine operations are limited to reordering and shipping after launch.
cards.use_when: Planning the ongoing workload of an Amazon FBA business after launch, or deciding whether FBA automation is worth it.
steps: Automate fulfillment by sending inventory to Amazon, letting Amazon pick, pack and ship orders (FBA) so you're not handling daily fulfillment.

After launch, identify the recurring tasks: monitoring sell-through, placing reorders with your manufacturer, shipping into Amazon, and light PPC management — that's essentially the source's ongoing workload.
Choose a manufacturer and shipping setup that doesn't require your physical presence; the source ran his business while living abroad and later in Mexico.
Keep supplier communication active to shorten reorder lead times, since that's where the recurring risk sits.
Plan for the launch to be the most work; expect operations to be lighter afterward if inventory and listings are set up well.
caveats: 'Passive income' applied to the source's later months — the 7-day setup was intense, and his own near-stockouts show passive still requires active reorder management.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx
